*This page is a reference, not a lesson. It answers one question: "I met
this term somewhere in the course; what does it mean here?" Each entry
gives a plain definition, the distinction most likely to cause confusion,
and the page that teaches the concept. Definitions follow the lessons;
where a term is used differently elsewhere in machine learning or
statistics, the entry says so.*

## A {#a}

### Activation function {#activation-function}

The fixed nonlinear function a unit applies after its weighted sum, such
as the logistic sigmoid, which squashes any real number into the range
between 0 and 1. Without it, stacked layers would still compute an affine
function of the input, so it is what lets a network represent nonlinear
relationships. The word "activation" is also used for the value a unit
outputs on a particular input; that value is computed from the input,
not learned, and is not a parameter.

*Taught in [Neurons, Layers, and Learning](learn/neural-networks.qmd) §4.
See also [affine function](#affine-function), [unit](#unit).*

### Adam {#adam}

An optimizer that adapts the step size for each parameter using running
averages of past gradients; the original Transformer was trained with
it. [S-42] Like plain gradient descent, it consumes the gradients that
backpropagation computed and performs the parameter update.

*Taught in [How Pretraining Works](learn/training.qmd) §4. See also
[optimizer](#optimizer).*

### Affine function {#affine-function}

A weighted sum plus a constant. Composing affine functions gives another
affine function, however many are stacked, which is why a network needs
a nonlinearity between layers. [S-15]

*Taught in [Neurons, Layers, and Learning](learn/neural-networks.qmd) §3.*

### Agent {#agent}

In this course, a system in which software repeatedly calls a model with
an updated context, executes the tool requests the model generates under
permission rules, and returns the observations for the next call, so
that the model directs its own sequence of steps and tool use within
constraints. [S-56] An agent is not a new kind of neural network: the
model inside is an ordinary transformer, and the agentic behavior comes
from the loop, the tools, the state, and the controls around it. The
word has no universally fixed definition; a system whose path is mostly
written in advance is better called a workflow. [S-50]

*Taught in [From Assistant to Agent](learn/agents.qmd) §4–§6. See also
[agent loop](#agent-loop), [workflow](#workflow).*

### Agent loop {#agent-loop}

The cycle that runs an agent: assemble a context from the objective and
the current state; call the model; receive either a tool request or a
response; check a request against permissions; execute it; place the
observation into the context; call the model again; continue, ask the
user, or stop. The model does not keep running between calls;
continuity is supplied by the context and state the software maintains.

*Taught in [From Assistant to Agent](learn/agents.qmd) §5.*

### Argmax {#argmax}

The single highest-scoring candidate. Selecting the next token by argmax
is deterministic and introduces no variation; softmax with the
temperature approaching zero converges to it when the top score is
unique. [S-10] Deterministic decoding can still produce unsupported
text.

*Taught in [Softmax, Sampling, and Temperature](learn/softmax-sampling.qmd)
§4 and §6. See also [sampling](#sampling), [decoding](#decoding).*

### Assistant {#assistant}

The product a person actually types to: a post-trained model plus a
system prompt, management of the conversation state, often retrieval and
tools, safety checks, and other product logic. It is not identical to
the model. Much of its behavior can be changed with no training run at
all, by changing what enters the context.

*Taught in [Post-training](learn/posttraining.qmd) §9. See also
[model](#model), [system prompt](#system-prompt).*

### Attention {#attention}

See [self-attention](#self-attention). When this course says "attention"
without qualification it means causal self-attention inside a
transformer block, one mechanism among several, not the transformer as a
whole.

### Attention head {#attention-head}

One instance of the self-attention computation, with its own learned
query, key, and value matrices. A transformer layer runs several heads in
parallel so that several attention patterns operate at once over the
same positions; this is multi-head attention, and the heads' outputs are
concatenated and passed through one more learned matrix. [S-37] Nothing
in the architecture or the training objective assigns a head a fixed,
human-readable job. [S-45]

*Taught in [How Self-Attention Moves Information](learn/transformers-attention.qmd)
§6.*

### Attention weight {#attention-weight}

The nonnegative number, summing to one across the permitted source
positions, that sets how much of each source's value vector is added
into a destination position, in one head at one layer. It is a local
mixing weight. It is not a probability that one token caused another,
and it is not by itself an explanation of the model's output, which
depends on every head, every layer, and the feed-forward sublayers.
[S-45]

*Taught in [How Self-Attention Moves Information](learn/transformers-attention.qmd)
§3 and §8. Not to be confused with a [weight](#weight) in the sense of a
parameter.*

### Autoregressive model {#autoregressive-model}

A model that predicts each token from the tokens before it, so that the
probability of a whole sequence is the product of one-step conditional
probabilities. [S-40] Generation appends each selected token to the
context and predicts the next; training evaluates every position of a
known sequence in one forward pass under the causal mask.

*Taught in [How Pretraining Works](learn/training.qmd) §1–§2.*

## B {#b}

### Backpropagation {#backpropagation}

The procedure that computes the gradient of the loss with respect to
every parameter, by applying the chain rule backward from the loss
through the network in one backward sweep, reusing values saved from the
forward pass. It computes gradients and does nothing else; a separate
optimizer step uses those gradients to change the parameters. [S-14]

*Taught in [Neurons, Layers, and Learning](learn/neural-networks.qmd) §9.
See also [optimizer](#optimizer).*

### Base model {#base-model}

A model that has been pretrained but not post-trained. Given an
instruction it may answer it, continue it, or produce more text like it,
because all of those follow such text somewhere in the training data.

*Taught in [Post-training](learn/posttraining.qmd) §1. See also
[assistant](#assistant).*

### Bias {#bias}

A parameter added to a unit's weighted sum regardless of the inputs,
shifting the result up or down. In this course the word always means
this parameter, not a statistical or social bias.

*Taught in [Neurons, Layers, and Learning](learn/neural-networks.qmd)
§2–§3.*

### Big-O notation {#big-o-notation}

Shorthand for an asymptotic upper order of growth as the input size $n$
increases. In the comparisons used here, $O(n)$, $O(n^2)$, and $O(1)$
stand for linear-order, quadratic-order, and constant-order scaling.
The course uses it to compare recurrent and self-attention layers.

*Taught in [Why Transformers](learn/why-transformers.qmd) §1.*

### Byte pair encoding (BPE) {#byte-pair-encoding}

A procedure for building a subword vocabulary: start from single
characters or bytes and repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair
into a new vocabulary entry, so that frequent sequences can become
larger vocabulary units while rarer forms can be represented from shared
pieces. Adapted from a data-compression algorithm; it sits between
character-level and byte-level units and whole words, and many current
tokenizers use it or a variant, often with a byte-level base. [S-27]
[S-28]

*Taught in [Tokens, Embeddings, and the Context Window](learn/tokens-context.qmd)
§2–§3.*

## C {#c}

### Causal mask {#causal-mask}

The rule, applied inside self-attention before softmax, that gives zero
weight to positions later than the current one, so a position can use
itself and earlier positions but never later ones. [S-22] It preserves
next-token prediction during training, when the whole sequence is
present, and it is what lets every position's loss be computed in one
forward pass.

*Taught in [How Self-Attention Moves Information](learn/transformers-attention.qmd)
§4 and [How Pretraining Works](learn/training.qmd) §2.*

### Compaction {#compaction}

Compressing or summarizing accumulated context into a smaller
representation so that work can continue with less context. Some systems
perform this automatically as the context nears its limit. [S-61] A
handoff is a deliberate, human-written state summary that serves a
related purpose; the two are not the same operation.

*Taught in [Using Models Well](learn/using-models-well.qmd) §3. See also
[handoff](#handoff).*

### Context {#context}

Everything the model conditions on for one call: the prompt,
instructions, the conversation so far, retrieved text, tool definitions
and tool results, supplied files, and the tokens generated so far. All
of it is tokens in one finite sequence, and none of it changes a
parameter. The course also calls it inference-time context, to keep it
apart from training. [S-31]

*Taught in [Tokens, Embeddings, and the Context Window](learn/tokens-context.qmd)
§8–§9 and [How Pretraining Works](learn/training.qmd) §8. See also
[context window](#context-window), [parameter](#parameter).*

### Context engineering {#context-engineering}

Managing what goes into the context at each step: the smallest set of
high-signal tokens sufficient for the next step, loaded when a step needs
it rather than all at the start, with stale or duplicated material
removed. [S-34] Named practices include just-in-time loading,
progressive disclosure, compaction, and handoffs. [S-61]

*Taught in [Using Models Well](learn/using-models-well.qmd) §3.*

### Context window {#context-window}

The finite sequence of tokens a model can reference when producing
output, including the output produced so far; its size is a fixed
maximum number of tokens that differs by model. [S-31] It is distinct
from the parameters and from the training data: each model step receives
a finite context supplied or managed by the surrounding system, and
products may persist information externally and supply it again on later
steps or requests.

*Taught in [Tokens, Embeddings, and the Context Window](learn/tokens-context.qmd)
§8.*

### Contextual representation {#contextual-representation}

The vector at a position after the network's layers have updated it
using the other positions. Unlike the token's embedding, which is the
same wherever the token occurs, it depends on the surrounding text: the
token ` bank` in "river bank" and in "central bank" starts from the same
embedding and ends with different representations.

*Taught in [Tokens, Embeddings, and the Context Window](learn/tokens-context.qmd)
§7. See also [embedding](#embedding).*

### Cross-entropy {#cross-entropy}

The loss that measures how little probability a predicted distribution
gives to the observed outcome. For a softmax distribution over a
vocabulary it is the same quantity as the negative log-likelihood of the
observed next token.

*Taught in [Neurons, Layers, and Learning](learn/neural-networks.qmd) §7
and [How Pretraining Works](learn/training.qmd) §3. See also
[negative log-likelihood](#negative-log-likelihood).*

## D {#d}

### Decoder and encoder {#decoder-and-encoder}

Two ways of using self-attention. An encoder lets every position attend
to every other, to represent a complete input; a decoder applies the
causal mask so that each position attends only to itself and earlier
positions, which is what an autoregressive language model needs. [S-22]
[S-24] When this course says "self-attention" without qualification it
means the causal, decoder form.

*Taught in [How Self-Attention Moves Information](learn/transformers-attention.qmd)
§4 and [Why Transformers](learn/why-transformers.qmd) §3.*

### Decoding {#decoding}

The rule that selects the next token from the probability distribution
the model produces: deterministically, by argmax, or stochastically, by
sampling. Decoding settings such as temperature change the output
without changing any parameter.

*Taught in [Softmax, Sampling, and Temperature](learn/softmax-sampling.qmd)
§6. See also [argmax](#argmax), [sampling](#sampling).*

### Direct preference optimization (DPO) {#direct-preference-optimization}

A preference-based post-training method that updates the language model
directly from comparison pairs, using a loss that resembles ordinary
classification, given a fixed preference dataset. It removes the
separate reward model and the online reinforcement-learning loop of the
classic RLHF pipeline. [S-47] Both routes remain in use.

*Taught in [Post-training](learn/posttraining.qmd) §5. See also
[reinforcement learning from human feedback](#rlhf).*

### Dot product {#dot-product}

The sum of the products of corresponding entries of two vectors of the
same length, giving one number. Self-attention uses it to compare a
query with each key.

*Taught in [How Self-Attention Moves Information](learn/transformers-attention.qmd)
§2–§3.*

## E {#e}

### Embedding {#embedding}

The learned vector that a token ID selects from the embedding table, a
matrix with one row per vocabulary entry. The entries are parameters,
adjusted during training so that prediction improves. [S-29] They are
not dictionary definitions, and nearness of two rows reflects
statistical relationships in the training text rather than a property
anyone specified.

*Taught in [From Text to Numbers](learn/how-created.qmd) §5 and
[Tokens, Embeddings, and the Context Window](learn/tokens-context.qmd) §6.
See also [contextual representation](#contextual-representation),
[token ID](#token-id).*

### External state {#external-state}

Everything the software or the tools persist outside the model: files
an agent writes, a repository, database rows, saved notes, stored
summaries. It can be read back into a later context, in this task or a
future one; doing so changes no parameter.

*Taught in [From Assistant to Agent](learn/agents.qmd) §7. See also
[state](#state), [memory](#memory).*

## F {#f}

### Feed-forward layer (MLP) {#feed-forward-layer}

One of the main computations in a transformer block: two linear
transformations with a nonlinearity between them, applied to each
position separately and identically, with no exchange between positions.
[S-38] [S-19] Named architectures arrange and order the block's sublayers
differently.

*Taught in [How Self-Attention Moves Information](learn/transformers-attention.qmd)
§7. See also [transformer block](#transformer-block).*

### Fine-tuning {#fine-tuning}

Further training of an already-trained model on new data, changing its
parameters. Supervised instruction tuning is one form of it; work on
pretraining and transfer showed that one pretrained model could be
fine-tuned for many different tasks. [S-24]

*Taught in [Post-training](learn/posttraining.qmd) §3 and
[Why Transformers](learn/why-transformers.qmd) §5.*

### Forward pass {#forward-pass}

Running the network end to end on a given input with the current
parameters to produce an output. During training it produces the
predictions the loss is computed from; backpropagation then works
backward through the same computation.

*Taught in [Neurons, Layers, and Learning](learn/neural-networks.qmd) §6.*

## G {#g}

### Gradient {#gradient}

For each parameter, how fast the loss changes for a small change in that
parameter with the others held fixed. Computed by backpropagation; used
by the optimizer.

*Taught in [Neurons, Layers, and Learning](learn/neural-networks.qmd) §8.*

### Gradient descent {#gradient-descent}

The update rule that moves the parameter vector a small step, scaled by
the learning rate, in the negative-gradient direction, the direction of
steepest local decrease. With a sufficiently small step this is locally
downhill; an optimizer need not update every parameter by a nonzero
amount. Pretraining runs this loop an enormous number of times on
mini-batches, usually with a more elaborate optimizer.

*Taught in [Neurons, Layers, and Learning](learn/neural-networks.qmd) §8
and §10, and [How Pretraining Works](learn/training.qmd) §4.*

## H {#h}

### Handoff {#handoff}

A compact state summary written to carry work into a fresh session or a
different model: the objective, the current state, the decisions already
settled, the source of truth, the open issues, the next bounded unit,
and what must not change. It replaces the transcript rather than
preserving it.

*Taught in [Using Models Well](learn/using-models-well.qmd) §8. See also
[compaction](#compaction).*

## I {#i}

### In-context (few-shot) behavior {#in-context-behavior}

A model performing a task from demonstrations or instructions placed in
its input, without any parameter update. GPT-3 was reported to do this
across many tasks, with the ability strengthening with scale. [S-26] The
course describes it as observed task performance, not as learning in the
training sense.

*Taught in [Why Transformers](learn/why-transformers.qmd) §5.*

### Inference {#inference}

Using a trained model, with its parameters fixed, to produce output from
a context. Request-specific information the model conditions on is
supplied through inference-time context; decoding settings and
surrounding product logic can also affect the resulting output without
changing model parameters. Training and post-training are the only
stages that change parameters.

*Taught in [How Pretraining Works](learn/training.qmd) §8–§9.*

### Inference-time context {#inference-time-context}

See [context](#context).

### Instruction tuning {#instruction-tuning}

See [supervised fine-tuning](#supervised-fine-tuning).

## K {#k}

### Key {#key}

In self-attention, the vector each source position is transformed into
for comparison with the destination's query; the dot product of query
and key gives the compatibility score. [S-36] One of three learned
transformations, with the query and the value.

*Taught in [How Self-Attention Moves Information](learn/transformers-attention.qmd)
§2–§3. See also [query](#query), [value](#value).*

### Key/value caching {#key-value-caching}

Storing the keys and values computed for earlier positions during
token-by-token generation and reusing them at each step instead of
recomputing them. [S-43] An efficiency measure that leaves the
mathematics of autoregression unchanged; cached tokens still occupy the
context window.

*Taught in [How Pretraining Works](learn/training.qmd) §9.*

## L {#l}

### Language model, large language model (LLM) {#language-model}

A model that assigns probabilities to sequences of tokens; the ones in
this course do so autoregressively, predicting each next token from the
ones before it. "Large" adds only scale. In the course's vocabulary
hierarchy, the LLM is the trained model, a transformer is its
architecture, and self-attention and the feed-forward layer are two
distinct mechanisms inside each transformer block. [S-19]

*Taught in [The Short Story](short-story.qmd) and
[Why Transformers](learn/why-transformers.qmd).*

### Layer {#layer}

A set of units computed in parallel from the same input, whose outputs
form a vector that is the input to the next layer. [S-12] In a
transformer the word is also used for the repeated blocks and for the
attention and feed-forward sublayers inside them.

*Taught in [Neurons, Layers, and Learning](learn/neural-networks.qmd) §5.*

### Learning rate {#learning-rate}

The small step size that scales each gradient-descent update.

*Taught in [Neurons, Layers, and Learning](learn/neural-networks.qmd) §8.*

### Logit {#logit}

In this course, and in machine-learning usage generally, the raw
pre-softmax score the network produces for each candidate token. This is
not the same object as the statistical logit function
$\log\big(p/(1-p)\big)$, which takes a probability and returns a real
number: an individual multiclass score $z_i$ is not $\operatorname{logit}(p_i)$.
The exact relationship holds only for differences,
$\log(p_i/p_j) = (z_i - z_j)/T$. [S-09]

*Taught in [Softmax, Sampling, and Temperature](learn/softmax-sampling.qmd)
§3–§4.*

### Loss {#loss}

A single number measuring how poor the model's current output is under
the training criterion; training adjusts the parameters to make it
smaller. For a language model the loss at a position is the negative log
of the probability given to the observed next token.

*Taught in [Neurons, Layers, and Learning](learn/neural-networks.qmd) §7
and [How Pretraining Works](learn/training.qmd) §3.*

## M {#m}

### Maximum likelihood {#maximum-likelihood}

Choosing parameters that maximize the probability the model assigns to
the observed training data; minimizing the summed negative
log-likelihood is the same thing. [S-05] Pretraining is
maximum-likelihood training, but it is not a conventional econometric
exercise aimed at identifying interpretable structural parameters or
reporting classical standard errors. [S-06]

*Taught in [How Pretraining Works](learn/training.qmd) §3.*

### Memory {#memory}

An ambiguous word that should be qualified whenever it is used. Three
different things get called memory: the model's parameters, which only
training changes; the current context, which lasts one call; and
persistent external state, which software stores and supplies again
later. An assistant that "remembers" a project has been given a file or
a store that is read back into its context; no parameter was updated.

*Taught in [From Assistant to Agent](learn/agents.qmd) §7 and
[How Pretraining Works](learn/training.qmd) §8. See also
[external state](#external-state).*

### Mini-batch {#mini-batch}

A small set of training sequences drawn from the training text for one
optimization step. Its gradient is a noisy estimate of the gradient over
all the data, which is why the procedure is called stochastic
optimization.

*Taught in [How Pretraining Works](learn/training.qmd) §4.*

### Model {#model}

In this course, a parameterized neural network that maps inference-time
context to a probability distribution over the next token. Pretraining
and post-training change it. A system prompt, retrieval, tools, and
product logic change the assistant built around it without touching it.

*Taught in [Post-training](learn/posttraining.qmd) §9. See also
[assistant](#assistant).*

### Multi-head attention {#multi-head-attention}

See [attention head](#attention-head).

## N {#n}

### Negative log-likelihood {#negative-log-likelihood}

The loss $-\log p(x_t \mid x_{<t})$: the negative logarithm of the
probability the model gave to the token that actually came next. It is
zero when that probability is 1 and rises without bound as the
probability approaches zero. Summed over positions, it equals the
negative log of the whole sequence's probability.

*Taught in [How Pretraining Works](learn/training.qmd) §3. See also
[cross-entropy](#cross-entropy), [maximum likelihood](#maximum-likelihood).*

### Neural network {#neural-network}

A function built from many units, each computing a weighted sum plus a
bias followed by a nonlinearity, arranged in layers, with trainable
parameters adjusted by training. [S-12] A transformer is
one neural-network architecture; a language model is a trained instance
of one.

*Taught in [Neurons, Layers, and Learning](learn/neural-networks.qmd) §5
and §11.*

### Nonlinearity {#nonlinearity}

See [activation function](#activation-function).

### Normalization {#normalization}

A step inside each transformer block that rescales the vectors so that
their values stay in a workable range through many layers. Where it sits
relative to the residual connection differs between named architectures:
after the residual sum in the original Transformer, before each sublayer
in GPT-2. [S-38] [S-39]

*Taught in [How Self-Attention Moves Information](learn/transformers-attention.qmd)
§7.*

## O {#o}

### Optimizer {#optimizer}

The rule that uses the gradients backpropagation computed to update the
parameters: plain gradient descent, or an adaptive rule such as Adam.
The optimizer performs the update; backpropagation does not. [S-14]

*Taught in [Neurons, Layers, and Learning](learn/neural-networks.qmd)
§9–§10 and [How Pretraining Works](learn/training.qmd) §4.*

## P {#p}

### Parameter {#parameter}

An adjustable number inside the model whose value is set by training:
weights, biases, embedding-table entries, attention projection matrices,
normalization scales, and the final output projection. Parameters change
only during training and post-training; they are fixed at inference
time. A value computed for a particular input, such as an activation or
an attention weight, is not a parameter.

*Taught in [Neurons, Layers, and Learning](learn/neural-networks.qmd) §1
and [How Pretraining Works](learn/training.qmd) §4.*

### Permissions {#permissions}

The rules in the software around a model that decide which requested
actions run automatically, which wait for approval, and which are
refused. They are enforced by the loop regardless of what the model
generates, and a well-behaved model is not a substitute for them. [S-54]

*Taught in [From Assistant to Agent](learn/agents.qmd) §10.*

### Policy {#policy}

In reinforcement learning, the thing being optimized. In the
post-training methods this course describes, the policy is the language
model itself, whose parameters are updated to raise a reward computed on
what it produces.

*Taught in [Post-training](learn/posttraining.qmd) §5 and §7.*

### Positional information {#positional-information}

Whatever mechanism lets a transformer tell the order of positions apart,
since the token embeddings alone carry none and self-attention has no
built-in notion of order. The original Transformer added a positional
encoding to each embedding; other architectures supply position
information in other ways. [S-30]

*Taught in [From Text to Numbers](learn/how-created.qmd) §6.*

### Post-training {#post-training}

Additional parameter-updating training applied after pretraining to
shape a model's behavior, capabilities, preferences, or safety
characteristics. It is a family of methods, including supervised
instruction tuning, preference-based methods (through a reward model and
reinforcement learning, or directly), model-generated feedback, and
reinforcement learning against checkable rewards; RLHF names one route,
not the family. [S-55] A system prompt is not post-training.

*Taught in [Post-training](learn/posttraining.qmd) §2.*

### Preference data {#preference-data}

Judgments about which of several candidate responses to a prompt is
preferred, collected from people, from models, or from rules, and used
by preference-based post-training. Different from a demonstration, which
supplies a single target response.

*Taught in [Post-training](learn/posttraining.qmd) §4–§6.*

### Pretraining {#pretraining}

Large-scale training on the next-token objective over a very large body
of text, updating the model's trainable parameters. [S-05] The targets
come from the text itself. The objective rewards assigning higher
probability to the observed continuation; independent truth verification
is not part of the objective. [S-08]

*Taught in [How Pretraining Works](learn/training.qmd).*

### Prompt {#prompt}

The text a user supplies for one request; part of the context. This
course treats a prompt as a task specification: the objective, the
source of truth, the inputs, the constraints, the required output, and
the acceptance criteria.

*Taught in [Using Models Well](learn/using-models-well.qmd) §2.*

### Prompt caching {#prompt-caching}

A provider feature that can reuse computation for a repeated input
prefix, reducing processing cost or latency on later calls. In the
implementation discussed in the course, cached input still occupies
logical context capacity: caching changes what the tokens cost, not
whether they count. [S-62] Pricing and caching behavior differ between
providers.

*Taught in [Using Models Well](learn/using-models-well.qmd) §11.*

## Q {#q}

### Query {#query}

In self-attention, the vector the destination position is transformed
into, compared by dot product with each permitted source's key. [S-36]
It is a learned projection, not a question; reading it as "what the
destination is looking for" is an intuition only.

*Taught in [How Self-Attention Moves Information](learn/transformers-attention.qmd)
§2–§3. See also [key](#key), [value](#value).*

## R {#r}

### Reasoning tokens (intermediate reasoning) {#reasoning-tokens}

Tokens a model generates before its final answer. On some difficult
tasks, generating intermediate reasoning tokens provides additional
inference-time computation and can improve performance; that is the
supported statement. [S-49] They are output produced by the same
next-token mechanism as any other output, not a transcript of internal
computation and not thought in the human sense.

*Taught in [Post-training](learn/posttraining.qmd) §7.*

### Recurrent network {#recurrent-network}

A network that reads a sequence one position at a time, carrying a
running summary, its hidden state, forward from each step to the next.
Relating distant positions takes many sequential steps, and the
computation cannot be parallelized within a sequence; that is what
self-attention changed. [S-16] [S-21]

*Taught in [Why Transformers](learn/why-transformers.qmd) §1–§2.*

### Reinforcement learning {#reinforcement-learning}

An optimization framework in which behavior is updated using a reward
computed on what the model produced, rather than by matching a fixed
target string. In post-training it is used with a learned reward model,
or with rule-based rewards on tasks whose outcomes can be checked.

*Taught in [Post-training](learn/posttraining.qmd) §5 and §7.*

### Reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF) {#rlaif}

Preference-based training in which a model, rather than a person, judges
which of two responses is better under written principles, and a
preference model trained on those judgments supplies the reward.
Constitutional AI is the published example. [S-48]

*Taught in [Post-training](learn/posttraining.qmd) §6.*

### Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) {#rlhf}

One route through preference-based post-training: train a separate
reward model on human comparisons, then update the language model by
reinforcement learning to score well under it while staying close to its
starting point. [S-46] Some writers use "RLHF" for any preference-based
post-training; this course uses it only for this route, and never as a
name for post-training as a whole. [S-55]

*Taught in [Post-training](learn/posttraining.qmd) §5. See also
[direct preference optimization](#direct-preference-optimization),
[reward model](#reward-model).*

### Residual connection {#residual-connection}

Adding each sublayer's input to its output inside a transformer block,
so that the sublayer computes an update to the representation rather
than a replacement for it. [S-38]

*Taught in [How Self-Attention Moves Information](learn/transformers-attention.qmd)
§7.*

### Retrieval {#retrieval}

Fetching relevant text from an external collection, a search, a file, or
a store and placing it in the context for the current call, so that
generation combines the model's fixed parametric knowledge with
information supplied at request time. [S-33] It changes the inputs to
this request, not the parameters. The published name for one such design
is retrieval-augmented generation.

*Taught in [Tokens, Embeddings, and the Context Window](learn/tokens-context.qmd)
§10 and [From Assistant to Agent](learn/agents.qmd) §7.*

### Reward model {#reward-model}

A separate network, trained on comparison data, that takes a prompt and
a response and outputs a score predicting how a rater would rank it;
used as the reward signal in the classic RLHF pipeline. It is an
imperfect stand-in for judgment, which is why the model being updated is
kept close to its starting point.

*Taught in [Post-training](learn/posttraining.qmd) §5.*

## S {#s}

### Sampling {#sampling}

Drawing the next token at random according to the probability
distribution the model produced, so that the same prompt can yield
different continuations without any change to the model. [S-07]
Contrast argmax.

*Taught in [Softmax, Sampling, and Temperature](learn/softmax-sampling.qmd)
§6.*

### Scaling laws {#scaling-laws}

The empirical regularity, reported for language models in 2020, that
loss improves as a power law with model size, dataset size, and training
compute over a wide range. [S-25] An observed regularity for the studied
setup, not a law of nature.

*Taught in [Why Transformers](learn/why-transformers.qmd) §5.*

### Self-attention {#self-attention}

The mechanism inside each transformer block that lets a position update
its vector using other positions: each destination's query is compared
with each permitted source's key, softmax turns the scores into weights,
and the destination receives the weighted sum of the sources' values.
[S-36] It is one of two main computations in the block, not the whole
transformer.

*Taught in [How Self-Attention Moves Information](learn/transformers-attention.qmd)
§2–§3. See also [transformer block](#transformer-block).*

### Skill {#skill}

A reusable set of instructions, procedures, examples, or resources
describing how to carry out a class of tasks, loaded into inference-time
context when relevant. [S-53] It changes what the model conditions on
for a task and leaves the parameters unchanged; it is not retraining.

*Taught in [From Assistant to Agent](learn/agents.qmd) §8.*

### Softmax {#softmax}

The fixed function that turns a list of real-valued scores into a
probability distribution: exponentiate each score, divided by the
temperature, and divide by the sum. Every output is positive, the order
of the scores is preserved, and adding the same constant to all scores
changes nothing. [S-01] Used at the output to obtain next-token
probabilities and inside attention to obtain attention weights.

*Taught in [Softmax, Sampling, and Temperature](learn/softmax-sampling.qmd)
§4.*

### Source of truth {#source-of-truth}

Where the answer to a question should come from: the model's general
knowledge, a supplied document, current documentation, a database,
running code. Deciding it before asking tells you what belongs in the
context and whether a tool is needed.

*Taught in [Using Models Well](learn/using-models-well.qmd) §4.*

### State {#state}

What carries a task from one model call to the next. Three kinds are
easy to run together: the parameters, fixed during a task; the context
window, reassembled every call; and external state, persisted by
software or tools.

*Taught in [From Assistant to Agent](learn/agents.qmd) §7.*

### Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) {#supervised-fine-tuning}

Post-training on pairs of a prompt and a demonstrated desired response,
using the same next-token loss as pretraining on the response tokens;
called instruction tuning when the pairs are instructions and answers.
[S-46] It raises the probability of responses that resemble the
demonstrations; it does not guarantee compliance or correctness.

*Taught in [Post-training](learn/posttraining.qmd) §3.*

### System prompt {#system-prompt}

Instructions a product places in the context in front of the
conversation, often carrying a persona and rules. It is inference-time
context: it changes what the model conditions on and no parameter, so it
is never a form of post-training.

*Taught in [Post-training](learn/posttraining.qmd) §2 and §9, and
[Tokens, Embeddings, and the Context Window](learn/tokens-context.qmd) §9.*

## T {#t}

### Temperature {#temperature}

A setting $T$ that divides every score before softmax. Lower values
concentrate probability on the top-scoring tokens and approach argmax as
$T \to 0$; higher values flatten the distribution toward uniform. [S-04]
It changes variability, not truth, and leaves the parameters untouched.

*Taught in [Softmax, Sampling, and Temperature](learn/softmax-sampling.qmd)
§6.*

### Token {#token}

A unit of text drawn from a fixed vocabulary: often a whole word, but
also a word fragment, punctuation, or another piece the tokenizer
defines. Not the same as a word; in many commonly used tokenizers a
leading space or a capital letter changes the token.

*Taught in [From Text to Numbers](learn/how-created.qmd) §3 and
[Tokens, Embeddings, and the Context Window](learn/tokens-context.qmd) §4.*

### Token ID {#token-id}

The integer index of a token in the vocabulary. An address, not a
measurement: the network never adds or compares IDs, and numerically
close IDs are not similar tokens.

*Taught in [From Text to Numbers](learn/how-created.qmd) §4.*

### Tokenizer {#tokenizer}

The program that splits text into tokens according to a vocabulary and
rules decided before training. Different model families use different
tokenizers, so the same text can be split differently by each.

*Taught in [From Text to Numbers](learn/how-created.qmd) §3.*

### Tool {#tool}

A capability the software around a model exposes to it: a name, a
description, and an input schema that the model reads, plus an
implementation that the software runs.

*Taught in [From Assistant to Agent](learn/agents.qmd) §2.*

### Tool call {#tool-call}

At the model boundary, generated output in a structured format
requesting a tool with specified inputs. The surrounding software
interprets that output, checks it against permissions, executes or
routes the action, and returns the result to a later model call; the
model does not itself run anything. [S-51]

*Taught in [From Assistant to Agent](learn/agents.qmd) §2.*

### Transformer {#transformer}

A neural-network architecture built from repeated blocks, each
containing self-attention and a feed-forward layer, with residual
connections and normalization. Transformer architectures are the
dominant foundation for many modern large language models; a transformer
is not the beginning of neural networks, and it is not the same thing as
attention. [S-19]

*Taught in [Why Transformers](learn/why-transformers.qmd) and
[How Self-Attention Moves Information](learn/transformers-attention.qmd)
§7.*

### Transformer block {#transformer-block}

The repeating unit of a transformer: an attention sublayer that moves
information between positions, a feed-forward sublayer that computes on
each position separately, plus residual connections and normalization.
[S-38] A model stacks many blocks.

*Taught in [How Self-Attention Moves Information](learn/transformers-attention.qmd)
§7.*

## U {#u}

### Unit (neuron) {#unit}

The basic computation in a neural network: a weighted sum of the inputs
plus a bias, followed by a nonlinearity. [S-12] Often called a neuron;
the course does not rely on the biological analogy.

*Taught in [Neurons, Layers, and Learning](learn/neural-networks.qmd) §5.*

## V {#v}

### Value {#value}

In self-attention, the vector each source position is transformed into
for transfer: the destination receives the weighted sum of the values,
weighted by the attention weights. [S-36] It is separate from the key, so
that matching and transfer can be learned separately.

*Taught in [How Self-Attention Moves Information](learn/transformers-attention.qmd)
§2–§3. See also [query](#query), [key](#key).*

### Vector {#vector}

An ordered list of real numbers of a fixed length. Embeddings, queries,
keys, values, and representations are all vectors.

*Taught in [From Text to Numbers](learn/how-created.qmd) §5.*

### Verification {#verification}

Making success observable rather than asserted: running the tests,
recomputing a number, rendering the document, reading the diff. A
passing test provides evidence that the specified checks passed. It does
not establish that the specification, research design, or resulting
number is correct.

*Taught in [From Assistant to Agent](learn/agents.qmd) §9 and
[Using Models Well](learn/using-models-well.qmd) §6.*

### Vocabulary {#vocabulary}

The fixed inventory of tokens a model uses, decided before training and
then never changed; typically tens of thousands of entries (GPT-2's had
50,257). [S-28]

*Taught in [From Text to Numbers](learn/how-created.qmd) §3.*

## W {#w}

### Weight {#weight}

A parameter that multiplies an input in a unit's weighted sum; more
generally, any entry of a learned matrix. Not to be confused with an
attention weight, which is computed for a particular input rather than
learned.

*Taught in [Neurons, Layers, and Learning](learn/neural-networks.qmd)
§2–§3. See also [attention weight](#attention-weight).*

### Workflow {#workflow}

A system in which the model calls and tool uses follow code paths
written in advance by a programmer; the model fills in each step but
does not choose the steps. [S-50] Contrast agent. It is often the
simplest system that reliably solves a task.

*Taught in [From Assistant to Agent](learn/agents.qmd) §4. See also
[agent](#agent).*
